newsitem.title: CONGO: Gunfire rocks Brazzaville for second day.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire rocks Brazzaville for second day.

text.p: Gunfire shook parts of the capital of Congo on Friday as supporters of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso clashed with the army for a second day, residents said.
"We've been hearing both light automatic weapons and mortar fire," an expatriate who lives in Brazzaville's business district said on Friday. "If anything, it seemed more intense this morning."
State radio said the army was in total control but an overnight curfew would be maintained until further notice.
The clashes broke out on Thursday after soldiers surrounded the home of Sassou Nguesso in the northern suburbs.

Sassou Nguesso, voted out of office in 1992 after the advent of multi-party politics, accused President Pascal Lissouba of fomenting the violence as an excuse to postone a July 27 presidential poll in the oil-producing former French colony.
Government officials in turn blamed Sassou Nguesso, saying troops had gone to arrest members of his entourage on murder charges but they resisted.
Unconfirmed reports said two soldiers had been killed and several civilians wounded, some by stray bullets.
Brazzaville emerged from a first night of curfew on Friday. Soldiers manned roadblocks in the centre of town and restricted movements of vehicles. Most people travelled on foot.

The road linking Maya-Maya international airport to the centre of town was blocked. An official with the airline Trans Air Congo said militias loyal to rival politicians and the army had been chopping down trees to make roadblocks.

Sassou Nguesso told Radio France International on Friday his supporters would resist any attempt to stop polling by force. "There is no doubt they will resist. We cannot accept that the process be put in doubt by force," he said in an interview.
Political parties armed supporters in ethnic and political fighting which killed 2,000 people following parliamentary elections in 1993. They were supposed to have disbanded.
Last Friday, the government formally banned private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms, and on Saturday party leaders meeting in Brazzaville pledged to avoid violence.
Clashes between supporters of Sassou Nguesso and former president and prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango in their home towns have killed 16 people in less than a month.
Yhombi Opango is Lissouba's campaign manager.

The government said it would pursue two senior members of Sassou Nguesso's guard it held responsible for the clashes. A government statement on Wednesday night also threatened tough measures against anyone carrying an unauthorised weapon.
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. Frontrunners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and Bernard Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.

France has economic interests in the Central African nation and 350 troops there -- left over from an operation to evacuate foreigners from Kinshasa in the last days of the civil war in former Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Brazzaville is just across the river from Kinshasa, capital of the former Zaire.

Sassou Nguesso ran a notionally Marxist single-party administration from 1979 until the advent of multi-party politics in the early 1990s. He then adopted an increasingly pro-Western foreign policy and liberal economic policy.
